To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
alerting modulated the congruency effects of a flanker task only when the spatial location of the target and distractor was different.
the alertness–congruency effect is modulated by the spatial relationship between relevant and irrelevant information.
the alertness–congruency interaction depends on the nature of the task and on the nature of task demands (spatial separation of information).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between alertness, executive control, and the spatial allocation of attention.
the interaction between alerting and attentional control.
the relationship between the alerting system and executive attention.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alerting improves performance in executive tasks by prioritizing spatially separated information.
alerting increases executive control by prioritizing the spatial location of the target.
alerting does not always increase performance on executive attention tasks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship between alertness (as indexed by the alerting task) and executive attention is not straightforward and depends on the specific executive task and its underlying mechanisms.
alertness is not an all-encompassing process that affects all aspects of cognition, but rather a specific process that affects only spatial processing.
alertness modulates executive control by prioritizing the processing of spatial information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
executive attention and alertness are related but distinct processes.
alertness is not a unitary construct. Rather, it is comprised of several distinct components.
alerting is a complex process that can have a positive effect on some executive tasks but a negative effect on other tasks.
